feedback: If the total jumps by six as each row is added, point out that this skip-counting by rows is exactly what 4 × 6 means.
If a learner still counts every tile one by one, slow down and highlight one full row, then count on by that row size instead of by ones.
After rotating, if the learner expects the area to change, re-count: the same squares are present, just turned, so the area is unchanged and 4×6 = 6×4.
If asked, show that going once around the edge (4 + 6 + 4 + 6 = 20) measures the border, not the covered surface — area is the squares inside.
activities.intendedInsight: The multiplication IS the array: one factor is how many squares are in a row and the other is how many rows, so rows × squares-in-a-row gives the same total as counting every tile. Rotation preserves area, which is why 4×6 = 6×4.
learnerActions: Set up a rectangle 4 rows tall and 6 squares wide, adding one complete row of six unit squares at a time.
As each row is added, count on by six: 6, 12, 18, 24, and notice the running total jump by six each time.
Alongside the growing grid, build the matching statement '4 × 6' and connect it to 'four rows of six'.
Rotate the rectangle so it becomes 6 rows of 4; check that the total is still 24, showing 4 × 6 = 6 × 4.
Say in your own words why you do NOT have to count all 24 squares — each new row simply adds another six.
activities.title: Build the array and watch the multiplication grow

feedback: If the grid is only partly drawn and the count seems off, mark the unit ticks on opposite sides and join them to complete every row and column, then recount carefully.
If the learner writes 4 × 6 but cannot explain it, ask them to shade one row and count how many squares it holds, then how many such rows fill the shape.
Praise an explanation that names 'six in each row, four rows' rather than just the right number.
activities.intendedInsight: Drawing and tiling your own rectangle, then writing the multiplication, cements that the two side lengths are the per-row count and the number of rows, and that their product is the area in square units.
learnerActions: On squared paper, draw a rectangle (for example 4 by 6) and tile it by marking off every complete row and column so no squares are missing.
Count the squares — first by ones to confirm, then by skip-counting whole rows.
Write the matching multiplication (4 × 6 = 24 square units) beside the rectangle.
Point to which side tells 'how many squares in a row' and which tells 'how many rows'.
activities.title: Tile and label on squared paper

feedback: If a learner accepts 4 + 6 = 10 as area, re-establish area by counting the covering squares (24) and contrast it with tracing along the edge.
Note that 4 + 6 = 10 is only two sides, and even the full perimeter 4 + 6 + 4 + 6 = 20 is the distance around the border, not the area — neither 10 nor 20 is the covered surface.
Confirm the correct area only once the learner shows the filled rows and columns giving 24.
activities.intendedInsight: Adding two side lengths (4 + 6 = 10) measures along the edge, not the covered surface; even the full border (4 + 6 + 4 + 6 = 20) is still a length around, not area. Area is the count of unit squares that fill the rectangle, found by multiplying squares-in-a-row by number-of-rows.
learnerActions: Look at a worked attempt where a child wrote 4 + 6 = 10 as the 'area' of a 4-by-6 rectangle.
Decide what 4 + 6 actually measures, and correct the method to find the true area.
Trace the border of the rectangle to see that adding sides follows the edge, while tiling covers the surface.
Rebuild the array and state the correct area, 24 square units, with its multiplication.
activities.title: Area is not the distance around (spot the error)

feedback: If a learner cannot yet see the row structure, do NOT impose a length×width rule — practise laying and skip-counting row-strips first, as spatial structuring develops with repeated array work.
If strips overlap or leave gaps, re-lay them edge to edge so every square is covered exactly once before counting.
Reinforce that each strip adds another six, which is why multiplying by the number of strips works.
activities.intendedInsight: Repeated equal row-strips make the 'rows × number-in-each-row' structure physical, so the multiplication is felt as grouping equal rows rather than a memorised rule.
learnerActions: Take strips of six joined unit squares (row-strips) and lay them to fill a 4-by-6 rectangle with no gaps or overlaps.
Count how many strips are needed (4), and how many squares each strip holds (6).
Skip-count the strips — 6, 12, 18, 24 — to find the total.
Write and say the multiplication: four rows of six is 4 × 6 = 24 square units.
activities.title: Row-strips that fill the rectangle

feedback: A full response names the two meanings of the factors and explains that rotation keeps the same squares, so area is unchanged.
If the learner multiplies correctly but cannot explain why, return to a drawn array and have them show which side is the per-row count and which is the number of rows, then skip-count the rows.
Treat a '4 by 6' area answer of 10 (two sides) or 20 (the full border/perimeter) as a confusion with distance around the edge, and reteach area as the covering squares (24).
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to justify the multiplication — not just compute it — is the sign the array structure has become the reason for the formula.
learnerActions: Answer why 4 × 6 gives the same number as counting all the tiles one by one, pointing to 'squares in a row' and 'number of rows'.
Complete a statement such as '4 × 6 = __ square units' and explain the unit.
Compare a 4×6 and a rotated 6×4 rectangle and state whether the area changes, with a reason.
Explain what a classmate measured if they wrote 4 + 6 = 10 for the area.
activities.title: Check and justify the link
